title: Running pilots without decisions, or committing to plans that cannot change
summary: Give each experiment a decision and keep the programme able to act on what it learns.
diagnosis: An endless pilot consumes attention without committing to adoption or closure. A rigid programme can create the opposite failure: evidence arrives but cannot change the roadmap. Maintain a durable business direction while allowing experiments to alter scope, architecture and priorities. Define what would count as useful learning and who has authority to act on it.
diagnostic_questions: What decision will this pilot enable, and when will that decision be made?
Which evidence would cause the team to stop, narrow the scope or choose a different approach?
What must be funded and owned for a successful pilot to become sustained use?
proposed_actions: State the hypothesis, uncertainty, resource boundary, acceptance evidence and scale/adapt/stop decision before the pilot starts.
Review results with business users and operating owners, including quality, adoption burden and integration effort—not only technical feasibility.
Keep a visible record of changed assumptions and retired work; require a new decision when conditions or system behaviour materially change.
working_artifact: Pilot decision record: hypothesis; users; task scope; baseline; evidence plan; resource boundary; decision owner/date; results; limitations; scale/adapt/stop choice; next operating commitment.
measures: Time from pilot start to a supported decision and proportion of pilots with explicit closure.
Conversion of validated pilots into sustained use, with reasons for non-conversion.
Resources redirected or risks avoided through evidence-driven changes, distinguished from arbitrary churn.
tradeoff: Frequent change is not the same as learning. A long project may be justified, and a stopped pilot may be valuable if it resolved an important uncertainty. Protected experiments still need an integration plan before their success can transfer to the core business.
illustrative_case: Illustrative application: a parallel support pilot improves first drafts but does not reduce resolution time. The decision may be to redesign the knowledge and escalation path rather than scale the current interface or abandon the whole opportunity.
